note.text: Earth is approximately spherical, with a slight equatorial bulge and flattening at the poles. Its mean radius is about 6371 km; its equatorial diameter is about 12756 km. A globe models this shape; a flat map represents selected features with some distortion. Evidence includes observations from space, a curved shadow during a lunar eclipse and changes in visible stars with latitude. A single local horizon observation needs careful interpretation because hills and atmospheric effects matter. Circumnavigation is consistent with the shape, but modern direct observation gives stronger evidence than an isolated travel story.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A pupil in Buea can compare a globe with a flat wall map. The map is convenient for routes, while the globe better represents the whole planet's shape. Neither is the planet itself. A ship disappearing hull-first over a clear sea can illustrate curvature, but one obscured view should not be treated as a complete proof by itself.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Separate an observation from the conclusion it supports. Use several independent lines of evidence. Do not confuse spherical with perfectly smooth: mountains and valleys are small surface irregularities relative to the planet. State whether a measurement is approximate rather than pretending every model is exact.
